title: cpu-side-bottlenecks-python-optimizations-threadpools
content:
Summary:

This doc summarizes profiling and microbenchmark work investigating CPU-side bottlenecks in the serving runtime. Primary suspects: tokenization, request parsing (JSON/validation), thread-pool contention, and Python-level overhead (GIL/serialization). Goal: prioritize mitigations that reduce p95/p99 latency and lower CPU cost per request for short text generation (avg tokens=40).

Background / why now:
- Customers hitting p95 latency spikes during bursty traffic; memory/GPU utilization looks fine but CPUs on frontends/routers are saturated.
- Recent deploy (concurrency changes) increased request parsing work and changed thread-pool sizing.
- We need low-effort mitigations before moving to bigger infra changes (dedicated instances).

Methodology:
- Collected perf traces (py-spy, linux perf) on serving-frontends under synthetic workloads that mimic real traffic (40-token responses, 1-5 req/s per worker).
- Used sampling CPU profiles and flamegraphs, combined with eBPF-based sched and lock analysis (bcc tools) to find lock contention and run-queue waits.
- Microbenchmarks run in containers to isolate components: tokenization (HuggingFace tokenizers python wrapper vs. Rust binary), JSON parsing (json.loads vs orjson vs yajl via C ext), request dispatch, and threadpool task scheduling.
- Measured wall time, CPU user/sys, context switches, and queue wait times.

Key findings (top-level):
- Breakdown (approx average, measured on c6g-like frontend instance): tokenization ~28% CPU, request parsing/validation ~18%, threadpool scheduling/queue-wait ~22%, Python GIL/overhead (serialization, call overhead) ~15%, serialization (msgpack/json for backend RPC) ~9%, other ~8%.
- Tokenization dominates for short responses where model forward time is small. Using HF tokenizers Python wrapper (calls into Rust) reduces cost vs naive python tokenizers, but overhead still high because we do tokenize for every request synchronously.
- Request parsing (JSON.parse + field validation) cost is non-trivial due to repeated schema checks and heavy use of Python dictionaries. orjson reduced parse time by ~50% vs builtin json in microbenchmarks.
- Threadpool contention: default threadpool size sometimes mismatched to CPU count; we observed high task queue wait times under bursts. perf shows significant time in futex/rcu waits and Python lock acquisition (lock contention on the task queue and on the per-worker request counters).
- Python-level overhead: repeated context switches between async event loop and CPU-bound tokenization/parsing cause GILing behavior; pure-Python helper functions (validation, small transformations) add up.

Representative numbers (synthetic workload):
- Baseline (current prod config): median latency 45ms, p95 220ms, p99 450ms. CPU usage per worker thread ~ 78% avg.
- Replace json.loads -> orjson: p95 reduced from 220ms -> 195ms (10.9% improvement), CPU/user reduced ~8% on parsing slice.
- Move tokenization to background worker (asynchronous offload) using a small Rust-based tokenizer service (local unix socket): p95 reduced 220ms -> 150ms (31.8% improvement), p99 reduced 450ms -> 300ms. CPU per frontend worker reduced ~25%.
- Increase threadpool worker count from 16->32 (on 32 vCPU host) without other changes: decreased queue wait but increased context switching; p95 improved modestly (220ms->200ms) but median slightly worse due to scheduling overhead. Shows we need smarter sizing and better scheduling rather than naive increase.

Root causes (synthesis):
1) Synchronous tokenization path coupled to request handler causes blockers: CPU-bound tokenization holds GIL long enough to stall other python tasks.
2) Conservative JSON parsing + per-request schema validation in Python creates significant per-request overhead; we parse and validate fields that are almost always present and simple.
3) Threadpool implementation uses a single global queue with coarse locks -> contention under burst.
4) Mis-sized pools and lack of backpressure cause queuing on the frontend threads, amplifying latency tails.

Mitigation candidates and tradeoffs:
Short-term (low-risk, ~1-2 weeks):
- Swap json.loads -> orjson for request parsing (low effort, safe): measured ~50% parse speed up in microbench. Owner: Evan. Expected impact: 8-12% p95 reduction.
- Add a fast-path for minimal requests: simple header detection that bypasses full schema validation when request shape matches (feature flag). Owner: Priya. Risk: correctness testing required.
- Add tokenization caching for repeated prefixes (LRU cache keyed by prompt hash) to avoid re-tokenizing user-provided prompts used in aggressive prefixing. Owner: Aisha. Expected: per-request CPU drop for common prompts, but cache memory impact needs evaluation.

Medium-term (2-8 weeks):
- Offload tokenization to a small native (Rust) microservice or native extension that releases GIL and runs in a separate thread pool (unix socket or shared library). Tradeoff: added IPC or native code surface. Measured earlier: ~30-60% CPU improvement in tokenization latency. Owner: Luis.
- Rework threadpool to per-core local queues with work-stealing (reduce global lock contention). Implementation: adopt existing lock-free queue (benchmark against current). Owner: Eng infra (TBD). Expected: reduce queue wait and lock time significantly under burst.
- Replace some Python validation with a generated fast C-extension or pydantic-core (fast compiled validators). Owner: Priya.

Long-term (>2 months):
- Rewrite hot-path request ingest in Go/Rust (thin proxy) that performs parsing, lightweight validation, and tokenization offload orchestration; passes normalized request to Python model-serving processes. High effort but would minimize Python overhead on frontends.
- Add continuous perf tests to CI that run microbenchmarks and collect baseline flamegraphs for regressions on PRs.

Experiments run / planned:
- orjson A/B on 10% of traffic for 48h (pass): no correctness issues, small GC pattern differences observed. Plan: rollout to 100% next week.
- Tokenization offload prototype (Rust service): benched locally with unix-socket -> p95 improved ~32%. Next step: small canary fleet test.
- Threadpool change: implemented prototype with reduced lock granularity; bench results promising in synthetic bursts but needs integration testing.

Action plan (concrete next steps, owners, dates):
- Week 1: Deploy orjson change to prod (Evan) and monitor p95/p99 (alerts for >10% regressions).
- Week 2: Implement tokenization LRU cache behind flag (Aisha), enable for canary and measure hit-rate and memory; if hit-rate >15% for top routes, expand.
- Weeks 3-6: Build/iterator on Rust tokenization offload and run canary on 5% traffic (Luis).
- Parallel: Threadpool redesign spike for per-core queues and lock-free metrics (Eng infra, owner TBD).

Open questions / risks:
- Cache correctness for tokenization when prompt includes dynamic instructions (must ensure no cross-user leakage).
- Native code introduces security/maintenance surface (audit + fuzzing needed).
- Interaction with autoscaling & latency SLOs: offloading tokenization may move CPU pressure off frontends to tokenizer service; need autoscale + request routing adjustments.

Appendix: profiling notes / commands used:
- py-spy record --native -o profile.svg -- python -m serving.frontend --load-test
- perf record -g -p <pid> -- sleep 30; perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg
- bcc tools: runqlat, offcputime to measure runqueue and off-CPU time
- microbench harness: bench/tokenizer_bench.py (compares HF tokenizers, orjson, builtins)

If no objections, I will: 1) schedule the orjson rollout, 2) create PR for tokenization cache flag, and 3) start the tokenizer offload spike. Feedback requested on priorities (should tokenization be our #1 focus vs threadpool redesign?).
